passage: Tuesday, 10 pm. Before I open a single book for the group report, I wrote what “done” means, on the first page of my notebook: (1) all four sections written, (2) numbers checked against the data sheet, (3) Raghav has read it once, (4) sent to the professor by Friday 5 pm. I've never done this before. Usually I work until it feels finished, and then it's never quite finished. I feel a bit silly staring at four lines, but they also feel like a fence around the work. Something has an end now. If Raghav's reading takes too long I'll still send by five. Friday 5:02 update: sent. It was good enough, and the evening is mine. — Sarika

qa.q: By what time on Friday did Sarika plan to send the report?
qa.a: Sarika planned to send the report to the professor by Friday at 5 pm.

qa.q: How does Sarika feel about the four lines on the first page?
qa.a: Sarika feels a bit silly at first but also comforted, because the four lines feel like a fence around the work.

qa.q: What difference did writing the endpoint make to Sarika's Friday?
qa.a: The clear list made stopping a decision rather than a drift, so Sarika sent the report at 5:02 and kept the evening free.

qa.q: How might Raghav feel about being one of the checkpoints?
qa.a: Raghav probably feels trusted and useful, and knows exactly what is expected: one reading, not an endless review.

grounding: A worker writes what finished looks like before starting, so there is no vague ninety percent.

passage:
Tejas: when do you stop working on something?
Charu: I write what done means first. for the sorting program it's: passes the three test files, comments written, emailed to ma'am
Tejas: that's it?
Charu: that's it. before, I'd keep tweaking forever 😅
Tejas: but what if it could be better
Charu: then it's version two. done is a promise to myself
Tejas: hmm. ok let me try for my lab record
Tejas: done = all 8 experiments copied, diagrams labelled, signed by Friday
Charu: love it. now stop at 5 on Friday 🙂
Tejas: even if I want to keep polishing?
Charu: especially then

qa.q: What does Charu's definition of done include for the sorting program?
qa.a: Charu's done means it passes the three test files, comments are written and it is emailed to ma'am.

qa.q: What does Tejas feel when asking whether it could be better?
qa.a: Tejas feels the pull of perfectionism and some doubt: “what if it could be better” shows a worry about stopping too early.

qa.q: What did Tejas write for the lab record, and what would it change?
qa.a: Tejas wrote: all eight experiments copied, diagrams labelled, signed by Friday, which gives a clear ending instead of an open-ended polish.

qa.q: How might Charu see the old habit of tweaking forever?
qa.a: Charu remembers it with a slightly embarrassed laugh and now treats “done” as a promise to Charu, so stopping is a choice.

grounding: A wise worker defines finished in advance, such as passing tests, commented and sent, so stopping is a decision.

passage: In the college hostel near Ahmednagar, Chinmay's field project on groundwater had dragged for three months the year before. This semester, before collecting a single sample, he tore a page from his notebook and wrote: "DONE means: 20 well readings taken, table typed, two-page report printed, signed by Nandini ma'am, one copy given to the gram panchayat office." He pinned it above his bed. In week six, the report was typed and he felt the old urge to keep tweaking the graphs. He looked at the page. Graphs weren't on it. He printed, got the signature and took the bus to the panchayat. At the office, he ticked the last line.

qa.q: How many well readings did Chinmay's list include?
qa.a: His list included 20 well readings.

qa.q: What was Chinmay feeling in week six when he wanted to tweak the graphs?
qa.a: He felt the old pull to keep polishing, a mix of habit and uncertainty about whether the report was good enough.

qa.q: Why did the written list help Chinmay stop?
qa.a: It set a clear endpoint in advance, so when he wanted to tweak graphs he could check that they were not part of done and move on.

qa.q: How might Nandini ma'am see Chinmay's project this time?
qa.a: She would likely be pleased and a little surprised to see him finish on time, after last year's project dragged for months.

grounding: Shows a student writing down in advance exactly what finished means so the project ends by decision, not drift.

passage: Clara had one rule for her statistics essays at university in Uppsala: before opening the data, she wrote a sticky note that said what done meant. For this one: "2,000 words. Three charts. Checked once for typos. Uploaded to the course site by Thursday, 5 p.m." Her friend Ingrid laughed at the note. "You're so strict." "Last year I had an essay at ninety-five percent for a month," Clara said. "It was never really done, just abandoned." On Thursday at three, Clara reached the typo check. She wanted to rewrite the conclusion again. She looked at the note, sighed, uploaded, and felt a surprising lightness walking to the café.

qa.q: When did Clara's note say the essay had to be uploaded?
qa.a: By Thursday, 5 p.m.

qa.q: What did Clara feel after uploading the essay?
qa.a: She felt a surprising lightness, relieved that stopping had been her decision instead of a drift.

qa.q: What could Ingrid borrow from Clara's method?
qa.a: Ingrid could write a clear definition of done before starting, with word count, checks and upload time, so there is no endless ninety-five percent.

qa.q: How does Ingrid see Clara's sticky note at first?
qa.a: Ingrid finds it funny and a bit strict, not knowing about the essay that sat at ninety-five percent for a month.

grounding: Shows a student writing what finished looks like before starting, so stopping becomes a clear decision.

passage: The college canteen committee met in a small room behind the kitchen. Mridul, a second-year student, had volunteered to run the survey on new menu items. Minakshi, the committee secretary, remembered last year's survey that never really ended. "What does finished look like?" she asked. Mridul thought, then wrote on the whiteboard: "Form shared with all hostels. 300 responses or Friday noon, whichever first. Results chart made. Presented at Monday meeting." She nodded. On Friday the count was 284. He wanted to wait for more. He looked at the board, closed the form at noon, and presented on Monday. The new lemon rice was on the menu by Wednesday.

qa.q: How many responses had come in by Friday?
qa.a: The count was 284.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling when the count was 284?
qa.a: He felt tempted and uncertain, wanting to wait for more responses to reach the number.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Writing an endpoint of 300 responses or Friday noon made closing the form a clear decision, so the results reached the menu quickly.

qa.q: How might Minakshi feel about this survey compared to last year's?
qa.a: Minakshi likely feels relieved and pleased, since this one had a clear end and led to a real menu change.

grounding: A student defines finished in advance on a whiteboard, turning the survey's end into a decision rather than a drift.

passage:
Hi Kashish,
Before we start on the robotics club's open-day stall, can I suggest something? Last year our stall was "almost ready" for three weeks and still half-built on the day. I think it's because we never said what "done" means.
So here's my draft of done:
1. The line-following robot runs a full lap on the test track three times in a row.
2. The poster is printed, not "on the laptop."
3. The sign-up sheet has a pen tied to it.
4. Both of us have explained the robot out loud to one person who isn't in the club.
When those four are ticked, we stop. No extra features, no "one more tweak." If we have spare time after that, we rest.
Does this list look right to you? Add or cut anything. Once we agree, I'll stick it on the lab door.
Amandeep

qa.q: How many times in a row must the robot run a full lap?
qa.a: Three times in a row.

qa.q: How might Amandeep have felt about last year's stall?
qa.a: Amandeep probably felt frustrated and a little embarrassed that it was still half-built on the day.

qa.q: Why does writing "done" in advance help the team?
qa.a: It gives clear endpoints like a printed poster and three clean laps, so stopping becomes a decision instead of a drift of endless tweaks.

qa.q: How might Kashish feel reading this email?
qa.a: Kashish would likely feel relieved and included, since the list is clear and open to changes.

grounding: Illustrates a student who writes what finished looks like before starting, so there is no vague ninety percent.
